primary_question: AI 및 데이터센터 확장이 전력수요와 전력망에 어떤 영향을 미치고 있으며, 그 영향의 규모, 시점, 지역적 차이와 인과적 확실성은 어느 정도인가?

items.fetch_note: Direct fetch of the base report page (https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai) was blocked by a provenance/permission gate in this session; the /executive-summary sub-page fetched successfully.
items.ai_attribution_rationale: IEA names AI as 'the most important driver of this growth, alongside growing demand for other digital services' but does NOT isolate AI's specific numeric share of data center electricity vs other workloads (crypto, general cloud/SaaS).

findings.fact: Global data centers consumed ~415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of world electricity consumption.
Regional split of that 2024 consumption: US 45%, China 25%, Europe 15%.
Data center electricity consumption grew ~12%/year since 2017, over 4x the rate of total electricity consumption growth.
Projected to more than double to ~945 TWh by 2030, and ~1200 TWh by 2035; US represents by far the largest share of the projected increase.

Up to ~20% of planned data center projects could be at risk of delay due to grid bottlenecks if risks are not addressed; wait times for critical grid components have doubled in 3 years; gas turbine lead times now span several years, potentially delaying commissioning beyond 2030.
In IEA's 'High Efficiency' scenario, data center electricity demand in 2035 is 20% lower than in the Base Case.

items.ai_attribution_rationale: Paper models general cloud computing (Meta, Google 2016-2022), not AI-specific workloads; relevant as a mechanism-level counterweight to 'efficiency will solve this' framing, not as direct AI electricity measurement.

findings.fact: Authors model cloud energy use as A = alpha*L*deltaPhi (efficiency x interface size x potential difference) and find energy consumption proportional to cumulative revenue using Meta/Google 2016-2022 data.
Despite hyperscale PUE reaching ~1.1 (near theoretical efficiency limit), Google's total energy consumption increased 3.7x from 2016 to 2022.

Conclusion: point-level efficiency gains (e.g., PUE) do not by themselves reduce aggregate energy growth because demand elasticity and reinvestment expand system scale (a Jevons-paradox dynamic); authors call for system-wide energy metrics rather than isolated efficiency metrics.
findings.status: ESTIMATED/INTERPRETIVE (authors' own argument, not an observed AI-specific measurement)

items.ai_attribution_rationale: Report attributes PJM demand growth to 'data center additions and electrification' jointly, not AI specifically, and the bottleneck it quantifies is on the GENERATION/interconnection-queue side (stalled renewables/battery projects), not a transmission capacity shortage.

findings.fact: PJM has roughly 130 GW of capacity-eligible generation projects stuck in its interconnection queue, unbuilt.
GridLab estimates customers could have saved ~$3.5 billion in the 2026/27 delivery year had just 10% of queued projects been operational.
The 2026/2027 PJM capacity auction cleared at $16.1 billion, up 10% year over year.
This is characterized as a generation/interconnection-queue supply shortage, not a transmission/distribution capacity bottleneck.
